idiom_name: durable_rules: Durable.ruleset + when_all blocks (Rete, C core)
implementation_notes: The durable_rules gem gives Ruby a production rule system: rules are declared inside Durable.ruleset with when_all/when_any condition blocks over the m (fact/event) name and consequences that assert, retract or post facts, all driving the same Rete engine (C core) that serves its Python and Node bindings. Forward chaining means facts asserted by one rule can trigger another, and correlated conditions allow rules over several events. State lives in the ruleset host, so scoping per request - or retracting facts - is what keeps a long-running process correct.
code_sketch:
require "durable"

Durable.ruleset :order do
  when_all (m.units > 100) do
    assert :subject => m.subject, :discount => 0.10
  end

  when_all (m.discount > 0) do
    assert :subject => m.subject, :free_shipping => true
  end
end

Durable.assert :order, { :subject => "A-1", :units => 250 }
pitfalls: The ruleset host is global state: facts asserted in one call remain visible to later ones, so a web worker needs per-request rulesets or explicit retraction.
Condition expressions compile to a deterministic state machine without backtracking: only the documented operators and matchers (comparisons, matches/imatches, array helpers) work.
Blocks run as ordinary Ruby when a rule fires, so rules loaded from an untrusted store are arbitrary code execution, not data.

variants.name: wongi-engine pure-Ruby Rete
variants.idiom_name: wongi-engine: triples + forall/has rules with production nodes
variants.implementation_notes: wongi-engine is a pure-Ruby forward-chaining engine based on Rete: facts are triples pushed into the engine (engine << [subject, predicate, object]) and rules are declared with a forall block of matchers (has, and the assign matcher for dynamically computed values), each producing a production node whose tokens bind the facts that satisfied it. It is the option when you want Rete semantics without a C extension, and the token API makes the matched sets first-class so a caller can inspect exactly which facts matched. The cost is a small library documented mainly through its tutorial: stick to the documented constructs.
variants.code_sketch:
require "wongi-engine"

engine = Wongi::Engine.create
engine << ["A-1", :units, 250]
engine << ["A-1", :loyalty_years, 5]

rule = engine.rule "volume-discount" do
  forall {
    has :order, :units, :units
    has :order, :loyalty_years, :years
  }
end

rule.tokens.each { |t| puts "discount for #{t[:order]}" }
pitfalls: The rule block is evaluated once and compiled into the network, so any plain Ruby expression inside it (Time.now, a method call) is frozen at definition time - use the assign matcher for values that must be computed per match.
The library documents no public API beyond the tutorial's constructs, so leaning on internals makes upgrades fragile.
Facts are untyped triples: a misspelled predicate simply never matches, so the fact vocabulary must be centralised.
